cards.front: What are the three main mechanisms that generate cardiac arrhythmias?
cards.back: Enhanced or ectopic automaticity (a steeper phase-4 slope or abnormal pacemaker sites); triggered activity from early or delayed after-depolarisations; and re-entry, where an impulse recirculates because of conduction block or slowing (circus movement or functional re-entry).

cards.front: What is the Vaughan Williams classification?
cards.back: A four-class scheme based on the main electrophysiological action: class I sodium channel blockers (subclasses IA, IB and IC), class II beta blockers, class III drugs that prolong repolarisation (mainly potassium channel blockers), and class IV calcium channel blockers. Many drugs act in more than one class, so the scheme is only a guide.

cards.front: Class IA antiarrhythmics: name the drugs and their main electrophysiological effects.
cards.back: Quinidine, procainamide and disopyramide block open-state sodium channels and dissociate with intermediate (moderate) kinetics. They prolong the action potential, refractoriness and QT interval, widen the QRS, and depress conduction. Their proarrhythmic risk, including torsades de pointes, is significant.

cards.front: Why is lidocaine a class IB drug, and what is it used for?
cards.back: It preferentially blocks inactivated sodium channels, so it acts mainly on depolarised or ischaemic tissue. It suppresses ectopic automaticity and ventricular arrhythmias, and it has practically no effect on atrial action potentials, so it is ineffective in atrial arrhythmias. It is given only intravenously because of high first-pass metabolism, and it has the lowest proarrhythmic potential of the antiarrhythmics.

cards.front: Class IC drugs: name the two main examples and explain why their use is restricted.
cards.back: Flecainide and propafenone are the most potent sodium channel blockers, with very slow recovery. They markedly slow conduction and widen the QRS, and they can be proarrhythmic. The CAST trials found excess sudden death with class IC drugs after myocardial infarction, so they are avoided in structural heart disease and ischaemia. Propafenone also has beta-blocking activity and is metabolised by CYP2D6.

cards.front: Classify: Class IB antiarrhythmics
cards.text: Class IB drugs such as {{lidocaine}} and {{mexiletine}} preferentially block {{inactivated}} sodium channels and are ineffective in {{atrial}} arrhythmias.

cards.front: Drugs for transient or acute atrioventricular block
cards.back: Atropine 0.6-1.2 mg i.m. when block is vagal (e.g. digitalis toxicity, some MIs); sympathomimetics such as isoprenaline in partial or complete block until a pacemaker can be placed. Drugs are only an interim measure until a pacemaker can be implanted.

cards.front: How do beta blockers suppress arrhythmias, and which arrhythmias respond best?
cards.back: They block adrenergically driven automaticity and after-depolarisations, and they prolong AV nodal refractoriness, which slows AV conduction. They work best in sympathetically mediated arrhythmias, inappropriate sinus tachycardia and AV-node-dependent tachycardias, and they control ventricular rate in AF and flutter. Long-term beta blockade reduces sudden cardiac death after myocardial infarction.

Asymptomatic or non-disturbing arrhythmias usually need reassurance only
Treat vigorously if life-threatening, haemodynamically significant, markedly symptomatic, or a warning arrhythmia after MI
ECG diagnosis and likely mechanism of the arrhythmia
Range of antiarrhythmic activity and pharmacokinetics
Haemodynamic effects and coexisting heart disease

Short courses are usual for acute problems

Sustained VT: amiodarone or sotalol; implantable defibrillator for prevention

cards.front: Short note: Drug management of atrial fibrillation

points: Relieve symptoms, prevent thromboembolism and prevent tachycardia-induced heart failure
Look for treatable causes such as hyperthyroidism
Calcium channel blocker (verapamil, diltiazem), alone or with a beta blocker
Digoxin is useful when heart failure coexists
Rate control (60 to 80/min) has given a better benefit-risk outcome than rhythm control in several studies
DC cardioversion is usual, and preferred in emergencies with hypotension or angina
Single large oral dose of flecainide or propafenone, once safety is shown under monitoring; IV ibutilide converts promptly
Maintenance drug chosen by underlying heart disease: flecainide, propafenone, dronedarone or sotalol with little heart disease; amiodarone (or dofetilide) in heart failure
Ablation if AF recurs or cannot be corrected
Dronedarone must not be used in permanent AF or advanced heart failure
Class IC drugs avoided in structural heart disease
Oral anticoagulation is essential for stroke prevention in patients at risk
Warfarin was standard; factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) and dabigatran are more acceptable alternatives

cards.front: Classify: Class III antiarrhythmics
cards.text: Class III agents include {{amiodarone}}, {{sotalol}}, {{dofetilide}} and {{dronedarone}}; the dose-dependent toxicity that limits sotalol is {{torsades de pointes}}.

cards.front: What is amiodarone's drug class and why is it called a multichannel blocker?
cards.back: It is an iodine-containing, very lipophilic, long-acting class III drug. It blocks delayed-rectifier K+ channels (prolonging repolarisation), also inactivated Na+ channels, partly Ca2+ channels, and gives non-competitive beta blockade, so it acts across several Vaughan Williams classes.

cards.front: Why does amiodarone rarely cause torsades de pointes despite prolonging the QT?
cards.back: Its action-potential prolongation does not depend on heart rate (no reverse use-dependence), so it does not lengthen repolarisation excessively at slow rates, which is the setting that favours early after-depolarisations.

cards.front: Main indications of amiodarone.
cards.back: Resistant ventricular tachycardia and recurrent ventricular fibrillation are the key uses. It is also used to maintain sinus rhythm in AF when other drugs fail, and in tachyarrhythmias of WPW syndrome.

cards.front: Amiodarone: list its main electrophysiological actions and its long-term benefit.
cards.back: It prolongs the action potential and QT interval by blocking delayed rectifier potassium channels. It also blocks inactivated sodium channels, partly blocks L-type calcium channels, and has non-competitive adrenergic blocking activity; its torsades risk is low despite QT prolongation. Its half-life is weeks. KDT notes that, apart from propranolol, it is the only antiarrhythmic shown to reduce long-term sudden cardiac death; however, its modest mortality benefit in heart failure seen in a meta-analysis was not confirmed in the SCD-HeFT trial.

cards.front: Short note: Amiodarone

points: Class III (potassium channel block) with class I, II and IV features
Very long half-life; slow onset on oral dosing, rapid on IV
Resistant VT and recurrent VF
Wide range of supraventricular arrhythmias, including AF maintenance
IV for rapid termination; oral for long-term prophylaxis
Oral loading of 400 to 600 mg/day for a few weeks, then 100 to 200 mg/day
Slow IV injection of about 5 mg/kg
Pulmonary alveolitis or fibrosis: most serious, less likely below 200 mg/day
Corneal microdeposits (reversible), photosensitivity and blue-grey skin pigmentation
Thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism, goitre) because of iodine content
Peripheral neuropathy; liver injury is uncommon
IV injection: hypotension and bradycardia
Raises digoxin and warfarin levels
CYP3A4 inducers lower and inhibitors raise its levels
Additive AV block with beta blockers or calcium channel blockers

cards.front: Classify: Dronedarone compared with amiodarone
cards.text: Dronedarone is a {{non-iodinated}} congener of amiodarone that does not interfere with {{thyroid}} function; it must not be used in {{permanent AF}} or in {{advanced or decompensated heart failure}}, where it increased mortality.

cards.front: Short note: Torsades de pointes and drug-induced QT prolongation

points: Polymorphic VT with QRS complexes twisting around the baseline
Usually associated with a long QT interval; may degenerate to VF
Early after-depolarisations after delayed repolarisation
Favoured by slow heart rates and pauses
Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia (e.g. diuretic use)
Bradycardia, female sex and structural heart disease
Use of more than one QT-prolonging drug
Class IA antiarrhythmics, amiodarone, sotalol
Terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride
Thioridazine, pimozide, tricyclic antidepressants
Quinine, halofantrine, sparfloxacin, moxifloxacin
Stop the culprit drug and correct potassium and magnesium
IV magnesium sulfate 1 to 2 g prevents recurrences even when serum magnesium is normal
Pacing or isoprenaline if bradycardia is present
Propranolol or esmolol IV may terminate the episode (KDT); defibrillate if unstable

cards.front: Adenosine: dose, route and mechanism in PSVT.
cards.back: Given as a rapid intravenous bolus over 1 to 3 seconds, usually 6 to 12 mg of adenosine (or 10 to 20 mg of ATP). It acts on A1 receptors to hyperpolarise SA and AV nodal fibres and reduce calcium current, which interrupts AV-node re-entry. More than 90% of AV-node-dependent PSVT episodes terminate within about 30 seconds. Its half-life in blood is about 10 seconds.

cards.front: Classify: Adenosine effects on the heart
cards.text: Adenosine acts on {{A1}} receptors to hyperpolarise the {{SA node}} and slow conduction in the {{AV node}}; its half-life in blood is about {{10 seconds}}.

cards.front: Why is adenosine given as a rapid IV bolus and why is its effect so short?
cards.back: It has a plasma half-life of about 10 s because red cells and endothelium take it up quickly, so a slow infusion would be inactivated before reaching the heart. A fast bolus terminates AV-node-dependent PSVT (over 90% within 30 s), but the brief action makes it unsuitable for preventing recurrences.

cards.front: Which drugs modify the response to adenosine, and why does it matter clinically?
cards.back: Theophylline and caffeine block A1 receptors and blunt its effect, so heavy tea or coffee drinkers may need higher doses. Dipyridamole inhibits its cellular uptake and potentiates it. Patients on carbamazepine have a greater risk of heart block.

cards.front: What are the main adverse effects of IV adenosine, and when is verapamil preferred?
cards.back: Transient dyspnoea, chest discomfort, flushing and a fall in BP are common. Brief asystole or ventricular fibrillation can occur and usually resolves quickly. It can precipitate bronchospasm, so verapamil is preferred in asthma. Its action is too brief for prophylaxis. Unlike verapamil, it is safe in wide-QRS tachycardia and in patients with hypotension or heart failure.

cards.front: Verapamil: which cardiac actions make it useful in PSVT, and why is it contraindicated in broad-QRS WPW tachycardia?
cards.back: It blocks L-type calcium channels, slows SA nodal firing and markedly prolongs AV nodal refractoriness, which terminates AV-node re-entry. A dose of 5 mg IV is given over 2 to 3 minutes. It is contraindicated in broad-QRS WPW tachycardia, where it can shorten the accessory pathway refractory period and speed conduction. Avoid it with IV beta blockers, in hypotension or heart failure, and in VT, where it may precipitate VF.

cards.front: Short note: Management of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT)

points: Vagal manoeuvres first: Valsalva, cold water to the face, hyperflexion
IV adenosine if vagal manoeuvres fail; it is the drug of choice
IV verapamil, diltiazem or esmolol as alternatives
Avoid with hypotension, heart failure or concurrent beta blockers
Contraindicated in broad-QRS WPW tachycardia
Oral verapamil, diltiazem or propranolol, alone or with digoxin
Catheter ablation for an anatomically fixed re-entry circuit or accessory pathway
Propranolol terminates PSVT less reliably than adenosine or verapamil
Adenosine's brief action makes it unsuitable for prophylaxis

cards.front: Case: PSVT in a patient with hypotension and heart failure on a beta blocker. Choose between adenosine and verapamil and justify.
cards.back: Choose adenosine. Its A1-mediated AV-nodal block is so brief that it is safe in hypotension, CHF, beta blockade and wide-QRS tachycardia, whereas verapamil depresses contractility and AV conduction and adds to beta-blocker effects. Reverse the preference in asthma, where adenosine can cause bronchospasm and verapamil is preferred. Doses may need raising in heavy tea or coffee drinkers (A1 antagonism), and be reduced with dipyridamole.

cards.front: Classical (stable) angina and variant (Prinzmetal) angina: how do their causes and drug approaches differ?
cards.back: Classical angina is caused by fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of epicardial arteries. It is provoked by exertion or emotion and relieved by rest, so drugs that reduce cardiac work help. Variant angina is due to recurrent coronary vasospasm, occurs at rest or during sleep, and needs drugs that prevent or relieve spasm, such as nitrates and calcium channel blockers.

cards.front: How do organic nitrates relax vascular smooth muscle?
cards.back: They are denitrated inside the smooth muscle cell to release nitric oxide, which activates soluble guanylyl cyclase. The rise in cGMP activates protein kinase G, which reduces myosin light-chain kinase activity and relaxes the muscle. Veins contain more of the mitochondrial enzyme that generates NO from GTN (aldehyde dehydrogenase), which may explain their venodilator preference.

cards.front: What are the main haemodynamic effects of nitrates in angina?
cards.back: Venodilatation pools blood and lowers preload, end-diastolic volume and wall tension, which reduces myocardial oxygen demand. Mild arteriolar dilatation lowers afterload. Large epicardial coronary arteries dilate, which can redistribute flow to the ischaemic subendocardium. They have no direct effect on heart rate or contractility, but a large fall in BP can cause reflex tachycardia.

cards.front: Sublingual GTN for an acute attack: onset, duration and key dosing points.
cards.back: The tablet acts within 1 to 2 minutes and peaks in 3 to 6 minutes because it is absorbed straight into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver. Plasma half-life is about 2 minutes, and duration depends on how long the tablet stays in the buccal mucosa. A usual dose is 0.5 mg sublingual at the onset of pain or before exertion. Pain not relieved after three tablets 5 minutes apart needs urgent review, since IV GTN may be started in acute coronary syndrome.

cards.front: Classify: Glyceryl trinitrate kinetics
cards.text: Sublingual GTN acts within {{1 to 2 minutes}} and has a plasma half-life of about {{2 minutes}}; oral GTN is largely inactivated by {{first-pass metabolism}} in the liver.

cards.front: Classify: Primary action of antianginal drugs
cards.text: Nitrates mainly reduce {{preload}}; calcium channel blockers mainly reduce {{afterload}} and improve {{coronary flow}}; beta blockers reduce cardiac work by lowering {{heart rate}} and contractility.

cards.front: Why is isosorbide mononitrate different from isosorbide dinitrate?
cards.back: Mononitrate is the active metabolite of the dinitrate: little first-pass metabolism, high and consistent bioavailability, half-life 4-6 hours. Its last dose is taken in the afternoon.

cards.front: Nitrate tolerance: when does it occur, and how is it prevented?
cards.back: Continuous exposure, especially with oral, transdermal, infusion or sustained-release therapy, blunts the haemodynamic and anti-ischaemic effects. Tolerance wears off within hours of stopping and is cross-tolerant between nitrates. Oxidative stress from denitration impairs the NO-generating enzyme, and neurohormonal compensation contributes. The main preventive measure is a daily nitrate-free interval. Intermittent sublingual GTN causes no significant tolerance.

cards.front: When must GTN be withheld in suspected myocardial infarction?
cards.back: When systolic BP is below 90 mm Hg, when heart rate is below 50 or above 100 per minute, and when right ventricular infarction is suspected. It must also be withheld if sildenafil was taken in the previous 24 hours. Nitrate-induced hypotension can also prevent the use of beta blockers, which have stronger long-term benefit.

cards.front: Why must nitrates be avoided after sildenafil?
cards.back: Sildenafil and other PDE-5 inhibitors raise cGMP, the same second messenger that nitrates act through. The combination can cause profound hypotension, and MI and death have been reported. Nitrates should not be given within 24 hours of a PDE-5 inhibitor, and a longer gap is needed after tadalafil because of its long half-life. If hypotension occurs, fluids and alpha-agonists are used for support. Other vasodilators add to the hypotension.

cards.front: Beta blockers in stable angina: how do they help, and which should be preferred?
cards.back: They lower heart rate, contractility and BP, cutting myocardial oxygen demand, especially during exercise. A slower heart prolongs diastole, which improves subendocardial perfusion. Total coronary flow falls slightly, but flow to the ischaemic region is not reduced. Cardioselective agents (atenolol, metoprolol) are preferred, since nonselective agents can worsen vasospastic angina. They reduce mortality after a recent MI and in heart failure, and in stable angina trials they gave better outcomes than calcium channel blockers. Abrupt withdrawal should be avoided.

cards.front: Short note: Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) in angina

points: Releases NO, which raises cGMP in smooth muscle
Venodilatation reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand
Dilates epicardial coronary arteries; mild antiplatelet effect
Sublingual tablet or spray: acute attack, onset in 1 to 2 minutes
Transdermal patch and sustained-release oral products: prophylaxis, with tolerance
IV infusion: unstable angina, MI, acute LVF; titrated with haemodynamic monitoring
Lipid-soluble; absorbed from buccal mucosa, skin and gut
Oral dose largely removed by first-pass metabolism in the liver
Half-life about 2 minutes; duration set by absorption and metabolism
Headache, flushing, dizziness, postural hypotension
Methaemoglobinaemia is clinically unimportant at usual doses
Tolerance and dependence with continuous use; withdraw gradually
Biliary colic and oesophageal spasm
Taken before meals in achalasia to reduce oesophageal tone

cards.front: Cyanide poisoning: which antidotes are used and why?
cards.back: Sodium nitrite forms methaemoglobin, which binds cyanide as cyanomethaemoglobin; sodium thiosulfate then converts cyanide to thiocyanate for urinary excretion. Hydroxocobalamin (high dose, i.v.) and dicobalt edetate are alternatives; hydroxocobalamin is particularly indicated in smoke inhalation (smoke contains HCN).

cards.front: Essay: Management of stable angina pectoris

points: Angina results from supply-demand imbalance; classical (fixed obstruction) versus variant (vasospasm)
Antianginal drugs relieve symptoms but do not alter the course of coronary disease
Sublingual GTN or isosorbide dinitrate as needed; sprays act faster
Beta blockers, cardioselective preferred; they reduce mortality after MI and in heart failure
Long-acting nitrates or long-acting calcium channel blockers as alternatives
Beta blocker plus long-acting nitrate: nitrate offsets tachycardia and ventricular dilatation
Beta blocker plus slow-acting dihydropyridine, especially if vasospasm contributes
Triple therapy for severe resistant disease; avoid verapamil or diltiazem with beta blockers
Ranolazine, ivabradine, nicorandil or trimetazidine as add-ons (trimetazidine second-line only)
Dipyridamole is not useful because of coronary steal
Antiplatelet drugs, statins, ACE inhibitors and smoking cessation

cards.front: Classify: Vaughan Williams class IV drugs
cards.text: Class IV agents are calcium channel blockers such as {{verapamil}} and {{diltiazem}}, which slow {{AV nodal}} conduction and prolong {{AV nodal refractoriness}}.

cards.front: Classify: Calcium channel blocker chemical classes
cards.text: The three CCB classes are {{dihydropyridines}} such as nifedipine, {{phenylalkylamines}} such as verapamil, and {{benzothiazepines}} such as diltiazem.

cards.front: Calcium channel blockers in hypertension: which agents are used, and what are their main advantages?
cards.back: Dihydropyridines, mainly amlodipine, are used most; verapamil and diltiazem are equally effective but less used. They lower BP by reducing peripheral resistance without reducing cardiac output or causing fluid retention. Advantages include no CNS effects, no sexual dysfunction, neutral effects on lipids, uric acid and electrolytes, and suitability in asthma, peripheral vascular disease and pregnancy. Short-acting nifedipine is not used for hypertension.

cards.front: Why is nimodipine used after subarachnoid haemorrhage?
cards.back: It is a short-acting dihydropyridine that crosses the blood-brain barrier well and acts on cerebral vessels; used to prevent and treat neurological deficit from cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage or ruptured aneurysm (30-60 mg 4-6 hourly for 3 weeks).

cards.front: Amlodipine: why does it cause few early vasodilator side effects?
cards.back: Slow oral absorption with peak level at 6-9 hours, more consistent bioavailability (less first-pass), and a very long half-life, so the blood level fluctuates little across the day.

cards.front: Felodipine: distinguishing features and approved use
cards.back: Greater vascular selectivity and larger tissue distribution than nifedipine with a longer half-life; approved for symptomatic treatment of Raynaud's disease; ER form once daily.

cards.front: Cilnidipine: what makes it different from other dihydropyridines?
cards.back: It blocks N-type (neuronal) calcium channels as well as L-type, and is claimed not to cause the reflex tachycardia seen with other DHPs.

cards.front: Short note: Calcium channel blockers in angina

points: Dihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine and others)
Phenylalkylamine (verapamil)
Benzothiazepine (diltiazem)
Block L-type calcium channels in smooth and cardiac muscle
Relax coronary and systemic arterioles
Verapamil and diltiazem also slow SA and AV nodes and reduce contractility
Effective in classical and variant angina; dihydropyridines suit vasospasm
Verapamil and diltiazem also used for arrhythmias and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Verapamil and diltiazem should not be combined with beta blockers
Short-acting nifedipine is avoided: reflex tachycardia and higher mortality after MI
Slow-acting dihydropyridines (amlodipine) are preferred; amlodipine is safe in heart failure
Not first-line in unstable angina; add to a nitrate when spasm persists
Dihydropyridines: flushing, headache, palpitation, ankle oedema
Verapamil: constipation, bradycardia, AV block
Verapamil and diltiazem raise digoxin levels

cards.front: Compare the cardiac effects of verapamil and nifedipine and explain the mechanism.
cards.back: Verapamil (and diltiazem) block L-type channels in a use-dependent way, so blockade grows with heart rate and recovery of the channel is delayed; they slow the SA and AV nodes and depress contractility. Nifedipine's block is independent of rate and it acts mainly on vessels, so it does not slow the node and instead causes reflex tachycardia. Hence verapamil suits PSVT and angina but is avoided with beta blockers, while a slow DHP can be combined with a beta blocker.

cards.front: Essay: Calcium channel blockers - classification and clinical use

points: Dihydropyridines, phenylalkylamines (verapamil) and benzothiazepines (diltiazem)
All block L-type calcium channels; dihydropyridines are the most vascular-selective
Vascular smooth muscle relaxation through reduced calcium entry
Cardiac depression (chronotropic, dromotropic, inotropic) greatest with verapamil, intermediate with diltiazem, negligible with dihydropyridines
Verapamil: use-dependent block, prolongs AV nodal refractoriness
Diltiazem: intermediate cardiac effects
Short-acting nifedipine causes reflex tachycardia; slow-acting agents do not
Angina (all classes); hypertension (mainly dihydropyridines)
Arrhythmias (verapamil, diltiazem); hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; Raynaud's disease
Dihydropyridines: flushing, headache, ankle oedema
Verapamil: constipation, bradycardia, AV block, heart failure
Verapamil with beta blockers: additive bradycardia, asystole
Raise digoxin levels; avoid in heart failure, sick sinus and second or third degree AV block
Avoid short-acting nifedipine in ischaemic heart disease

cards.front: Trimetazidine: how does it work, and why is it not a haemodynamic drug?
cards.back: It inhibits long-chain 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (LC3-KAT), a key enzyme of fatty acid oxidation. Myocardium shifts toward glucose oxidation, which needs less oxygen per unit of ATP. It has no effect on heart rate or BP at rest or on exercise, yet it reduces angina frequency and increases exercise capacity. Side effects include GI upset; it can cause movement disorders such as parkinsonism, especially in the elderly; GG14 lists it as a second-choice add-on for exertional angina. It is not approved in the USA.

cards.front: Nicorandil: mechanism and main adverse effects.
cards.back: It opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in smooth muscle, causing hyperpolarisation, and it also acts as a nitric oxide donor that raises cGMP. It lowers preload and afterload and increases coronary flow, with no significant effect on contractility or conduction. Adverse effects include flushing, headache, palpitation and painful oral aphthous ulcers. Concurrent PDE-5 inhibitors are contraindicated, and it does not cause nitrate-type tolerance.

cards.front: Classify: Dipyridamole and coronary steal
cards.text: Dipyridamole raises total coronary flow but causes {{coronary steal}} by dilating non-ischaemic resistance vessels, so it is not an effective {{antianginal}} drug; it is used as an adjunct {{antiplatelet}} agent.

cards.front: Classify: Drugs for peripheral vascular disease
cards.text: {{Cilostazol}} is a {{PDE-3}} inhibitor used for intermittent {{claudication}}; {{pentoxifylline}} acts mainly by reducing {{blood viscosity}}.

cards.front: Cilostazol: mechanism, indication and key cautions
cards.back: PDE-3 inhibitor raising cAMP in platelets and vascular smooth muscle; used only for intermittent claudication without rest pain; avoid in heart failure; CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 inhibitors increase toxicity.

cards.front: Pentoxifylline: how does it help intermittent claudication?
cards.back: Acts mainly on rheology: lowers whole-blood viscosity and improves red cell flexibility, improving microcirculatory flow without a major change in heart rate, total peripheral resistance or BP.

cards.front: Ranolazine: mechanism, effect on heart rate and BP, and key safety issues.
cards.back: It inhibits the late sodium current, which indirectly reduces calcium overload during ischaemia and helps preserve myocardial function. It does not change heart rate or BP, and it prolongs exercise duration. It prolongs the QT interval, so it must not be combined with other QT-prolonging drugs, and CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided. It can be used with sildenafil.

cards.front: Short note: Ivabradine

points: Selective blockade of the funny (If) current in the SA node
Slows diastolic depolarisation and lowers heart rate without negative inotropy
Chronic stable angina when beta blockers are contraindicated, not tolerated or insufficiently effective (EMA approval; in the USA it is approved only for heart failure)
Symptomatic inappropriate sinus tachycardia, when beta blockers and verapamil are unsuitable
Stable chronic systolic heart failure in sinus rhythm at 70/min or more, added to standard therapy
Resting heart rate below 60/min, sick sinus syndrome, AF
Concurrent QT-prolonging drugs or CYP3A4 inhibitors
Phosphenes: transient brightness in part of the visual field, from block of retinal HCN channels
Bradycardia, ectopic beats, PR prolongation, headache, dizziness, nausea
Adding it to beta blockers in chronic angina gave no benefit and more bradycardia, AF and QT prolongation

cards.front: Short note: Drug therapy of acute myocardial infarction

points: GTN; if pain persists after three doses, IV morphine or diazepam
Oxygen if hypoxic; correct acidosis with IV bicarbonate if needed
Avoid volume overload; furosemide if pulmonary wedge pressure is high
Dopamine or dobutamine for pump failure
Early beta blocker if no contraindication; reduces infarct size and arrhythmias
Lidocaine, procainamide or amiodarone for VT; atropine or pacing for bradycardia
Routine prophylactic lidocaine is no longer recommended
Aspirin 162 to 325 mg chewed at once, then 80 to 160 mg daily
Clopidogrel, prasugrel or ticagrelor as add-on antiplatelets
Fibrinolysis for STEMI within 1 to 2 hours of onset, otherwise primary PCI
ACE inhibitors or ARBs for remodelling and survival
Long-term beta blocker, statin and antiplatelet therapy for secondary prevention

cards.front: How do the major guidelines define hypertension and set treatment thresholds (NICE 2011, JNC 8, ACC/AHA 2017, ESC 2018)?
cards.back: NICE 2011 (as in KDT): stage I 140 to 159/90 to 99, stage II 160 to 179/100 to 109, severe 180/110 mm Hg or more. JNC 8 (2014): treat from 140/90, except in people aged 60 or over, where the systolic threshold and goal are 150 mm Hg (diastolic stays 90). ACC/AHA 2017: normal below 120/80, elevated 120 to 129/below 80, stage 1 130 to 139/80 to 89, stage 2 140/90 or more; so hypertension in the USA starts at 130/80 and the target is below 130/80, with drugs in stage 1 only if there is atherosclerotic disease or a 10-year risk of 10% or more. ESC 2018: hypertension remains 140/90 or more, with a systolic target below 140 and close to 130. The lower targets followed SPRINT, where a systolic target of 120 rather than 140 mm Hg cut cardiovascular events and total mortality by about 25%.

cards.front: Thiazide diuretics: the usual antihypertensive dose and why higher doses are avoided.
cards.back: Low-dose hydrochlorothiazide (12.5 to 25 mg/day) or chlorthalidone is preferred. Maximal antihypertensive effect is reached at 25 mg/day, which gives the best benefit-risk ratio; higher doses mainly add adverse effects. Higher doses cause hypokalaemia, glucose intolerance, dyslipidaemia and hyperuricaemia without much further BP fall. Thiazides are ineffective in advanced chronic kidney disease.

cards.front: Clonidine: mechanism of action and the withdrawal syndrome.
cards.back: Clonidine is a central alpha-2A agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow from the medulla, lowering BP and heart rate. Stopping it abruptly, especially after missed doses, can cause severe rebound hypertension with tachycardia, anxiety, sweating and headache, resembling phaeochromocytoma. It is treated with an alpha plus beta blocker, nitroprusside, or clonidine itself. Tricyclic antidepressants antagonise its effect.

cards.front: Methyldopa: active metabolite, site of action, and why it is used in pregnancy.
cards.back: Methyldopa is converted in the body to alpha-methylnoradrenaline, a central alpha-2 agonist that lowers sympathetic tone and reduces total peripheral resistance more than heart rate or output. It is now used mainly in pregnancy because of its long safety record. Sedation and mental slowing are common. A positive Coombs test is common, but haemolytic anaemia is rare.

cards.front: Hydralazine: mechanism, reflex effects, and main limitations.
cards.back: It is a direct arteriolar vasodilator with little venous action, so it lowers diastolic BP more than systolic. Baroreflex activation causes tachycardia, higher cardiac output and renin release, leading to salt and water retention and tolerance unless a diuretic or beta blocker is added. It can provoke angina. Prolonged use above 100 mg/day can cause a lupus-like syndrome, more often in women and slow acetylators.

cards.front: Reserpine: mechanism and why it is no longer used as an antihypertensive.
cards.back: Reserpine irreversibly inhibits the vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2), so noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin are gradually lost and degraded. The effect outlasts the drug for weeks. Central depletion causes sedation, depression and extrapyramidal symptoms. It has been replaced by safer agents and is now used mainly as a pharmacological tool.

cards.front: Classify: Central and neuronal antihypertensives
cards.text: {{Clonidine}} and {{methyldopa}} act as central {{alpha-2}} agonists, while {{reserpine}} depletes monoamines by blocking the {{vesicular monoamine transporter}}.

cards.front: Classify: Direct vasodilator antihypertensives
cards.text: {{Hydralazine}} is a direct arteriolar vasodilator that provokes {{reflex tachycardia}} and fluid retention, while {{minoxidil}} acts by opening {{ATP-sensitive potassium}} channels in smooth muscle.

cards.front: Classify: Diuretics and aldosterone antagonists
cards.text: Low-dose {{hydrochlorothiazide}} (12.5 to 25 mg/day) is first-line; {{spironolactone}} and {{eplerenone}} are aldosterone antagonists that reduce potassium loss but can cause {{hyperkalaemia}} with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

cards.front: Guanethidine: mechanism and status
cards.back: Polar guanidine taken up into adrenergic nerve endings by amine transport, where it blocks impulse-coupled noradrenaline release; out of use now because of marked side effects.

cards.front: Clonidine: uses other than hypertension
cards.back: Opioid withdrawal (suppresses sympathetic overactivity and craving), analgesia (intrathecal or epidural), menopausal vasomotor symptoms, and diarrhoea from diabetic neuropathy.

cards.front: Minoxidil: why is it used topically?
cards.back: Oral minoxidil is no longer used because of vasodilator effects and cardiac risk; 2% topical solution applied twice daily promotes hair growth in male pattern baldness and alopecia areata, with a slow, incomplete response that is lost on stopping.

cards.front: ACE inhibitors in hypertension: where are they preferred, and what is the main limiting adverse effect?
cards.back: They are first-line in most grades of essential and renovascular hypertension, except bilateral renal artery stenosis. They are preferred with diabetes, nephropathy, left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, angina and after MI. Dry, persistent cough, from raised bradykinin, is the most common reason to stop them. They are contraindicated in pregnancy.

cards.front: ARBs compared with ACE inhibitors: practical advantages, and which combination is discouraged?
cards.back: ARBs block the angiotensin receptor without raising kinin levels, so the ACE inhibitor cough is avoided; angioedema and taste disturbance are rare. They share the metabolic and prognostic benefits of ACE inhibitors. JNC 8 and NICE advise against combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB. ARBs are also avoided in pregnancy.

cards.front: Beta blockers in hypertension: why are they no longer first-line?
cards.back: They are mild antihypertensives, and in primary prevention they are less effective than diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs for stroke and MI. Nonselective agents raise triglycerides and worsen quality of life, and rebound hypertension and angina can follow abrupt withdrawal. They remain indicated for compelling reasons such as post-MI, stable heart failure or high coronary risk.

cards.front: Short note: Adverse effects of thiazide diuretics and the low-dose approach

points: Hypokalaemia with cramps and fatigue
Impaired glucose tolerance, dyslipidaemia and hyperuricaemia (gout)
Erectile dysfunction; sudden cardiac death was linked to hypokalaemia at higher doses
12.5 to 25 mg/day causes little hypokalaemia; ECG studies showed no excess arrhythmia
Metabolic effects are minimal; not contraindicated in diabetes
Reduces fatal and non-fatal MI and stroke in trials
Monitor potassium; add a potassium-sparing agent if needed
NSAIDs weaken the antihypertensive effect
Ineffective in chronic kidney disease

cards.front: Resistant hypertension: common causes and drug approach
cards.back: Many patients need two, three or four drugs at optimal doses. Common reasons for apparent resistance are inadequate doses, poor adherence, combining drugs that act by the same mechanism, high salt intake and salt retention caused by vasodilators (so diuretic therapy is often inadequate), and interfering drugs: NSAIDs, sympathomimetic decongestants, ciclosporin, erythropoietin, ephedra, liquorice, cocaine and amphetamines. Many resistant patients have primary hyperaldosteronism and respond to adding spironolactone 25 to 50 mg daily; alternatives at this step are another diuretic, an alpha-1 blocker or a beta blocker. Renal denervation may help selected patients with well-defined resistant hypertension.

cards.front: Short note: Principles of choosing an antihypertensive for an individual patient

points: Decide on BP level plus target-organ damage and total cardiovascular risk
Risk factors: age over 55 (men) or 65 (women), smoking, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, CKD, obesity
Lifestyle measures are started together with drugs
Heart failure, post-MI, diabetes, CKD and recurrent stroke each favour particular classes
A compelling indication can justify a drug and a lower BP target even near normal BP
Young non-black patients: thiazide, ACE inhibitor/ARB or CCB as initial drug
Older patients and blacks of any age: thiazide or CCB first, as renin is lower and ACE inhibitor response weaker
Add a second drug in steps if target is not reached
Beta blocker with diuretic (raises diabetes risk)
ACE inhibitor with ARB
Verapamil or diltiazem with beta blocker (bradycardia, AV block)
Alpha or beta blocker with clonidine (blunts clonidine)
Pregnancy: avoid ACE inhibitors and ARBs (fetal damage); diuretics can reduce uteroplacental flow
Lower BP gradually; a sudden fall can reduce perfusion
CCBs are not contraindicated in asthma, angina or peripheral vascular disease

cards.front: Short note: Clonidine

points: Imidazoline with partial agonism at alpha-2A receptors, mainly in the brainstem
Lowers central sympathetic outflow from the medulla: fall in BP and heart rate
Enhanced vagal tone adds to bradycardia; plasma noradrenaline falls
Well absorbed orally; peak in 2 to 4 hours
One-half to two-thirds of an oral dose excreted unchanged in urine
Plasma half-life 8 to 12 hours; single dose acts for 6 to 24 hours
Once a popular antihypertensive; now third or fourth choice
Limited by side effects, withdrawal hypertension and tolerance
Occasionally added to a diuretic
Opioid and alcohol withdrawal, smoking cessation, analgesic adjunct, menopausal flushing, diabetic diarrhoea
Sedation, dry mouth, constipation, impotence, salt and water retention, bradycardia, postural hypotension
Missed doses for 1 to 2 days can cause rebound hypertension with tachycardia, anxiety, sweating and headache, like phaeochromocytoma
Treat with alpha plus beta blocker, nitroprusside, or clonidine itself
Tricyclic antidepressants and chlorpromazine abolish its antihypertensive effect

cards.front: Prazosin: why is the first dose given at bedtime and kept low?
cards.back: Starting at 0.5 mg at bedtime limits the first-dose effect of postural hypotension and fainting, which is greatest at the start and with dose increments.

cards.front: Short note: Stepped drug therapy of hypertension (NICE 2011, JNC 8 and ESC 2018)

points: NICE 2011 (KDT): ACE inhibitor or ARB under 55 years; CCB at 55 or over and in black patients of any age; thiazide if a CCB is unsuitable
JNC 8: thiazide, ACE inhibitor/ARB or CCB for non-blacks; thiazide or CCB for blacks
ESC 2018 (GG14): start most patients on a single-pill two-drug combination (ACE inhibitor or ARB plus CCB or diuretic); ACC/AHA advise this when BP is more than 20/10 above goal
Two drugs: ACE inhibitor/ARB plus CCB, or diuretic if CCB unsuitable
If a beta blocker was started, add a CCB as the second drug
ACE inhibitor/ARB plus CCB plus thiazide, after titrating existing doses
NICE 2011: add an aldosterone antagonist if K+ is below 4.5 mmol/L, or a higher thiazide dose if K+ is above 4.5
ESC 2018: add spironolactone 25 to 50 mg daily, or another diuretic, an alpha-1 blocker or a beta blocker
Beta blockers can be used at any step when there is a specific indication
ACE inhibitor with ARB
Verapamil or diltiazem with a beta blocker
Beta blocker with a diuretic (diabetes risk)
Alpha or beta blocker with clonidine; hydralazine with a dihydropyridine or prazosin

cards.front: Essay: Management of essential hypertension - selecting drugs

points: Hypertension defined by BP level; risk depends also on other factors and target-organ damage
Essential (primary) hypertension accounts for most cases
Salt restriction, weight reduction, exercise, moderation of alcohol, stress reduction
Treat a secondary cause if identified
Heart failure, post-MI, diabetes, CKD, recurrent stroke, stable angina
Choose the class with proven benefit for that indication
Chosen by age, race and renin status
Thiazides, ACE inhibitors/ARBs and CCBs are the first-line classes; beta blockers only for compelling indications
Targets: below 130/80 (ACC/AHA 2017) or systolic below 140 and close to 130 (ESC 2018); JNC 8 below 150/90 at 60 or over
Step 2: two drugs; step 3: three first-line classes; step 4: resistant hypertension
Titrate existing doses before adding a further drug
Early single-pill combination therapy is a common recommendation of current guidelines
Pregnancy, elderly patients, diabetics, CKD and black patients need tailored choices
Reduce BP gradually where organ damage exists, to the level tolerated

cards.front: Essay: Classification of antihypertensive drugs

points: Thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide)
High-ceiling diuretics for CKD or refractory oedema
Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone)
ACE inhibitors (enalapril, ramipril)
ARBs (losartan, valsartan, candesartan)
Direct renin inhibitor (aliskiren)
Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine SR)
Verapamil and diltiazem
Cardioselective (atenolol, metoprolol)
Vasodilating (nebivolol, carvedilol)
Prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin
Labetalol (alpha plus beta)
Clonidine and methyldopa (central alpha-2 action)
Reserpine (monoamine depletion)
Hydralazine, minoxidil, sodium nitroprusside

cards.front: Short note: Third-generation beta blockers with vasodilatation

points: Beta blockers that also dilate blood vessels, beyond blocking beta receptors
Extra vasodilatation comes mainly from nitric oxide (NO) release or alpha-1 blockade
Nebivolol: activates endothelial NO synthase; vasodilates; does not worsen lipids or glucose
Nebivolol dose 5 mg once daily (2.5 mg in elderly)
Celiprolol: weak beta-2 agonism; NO-mediated vasodilatation adds to BP fall
Carvedilol: alpha-1 blockade plus calcium-entry blockade; antioxidant action
Labetalol and bucindolol: alpha-1 blockade with beta blockade (grouped with carvedilol)
Hypertension for nebivolol, celiprolol and carvedilol
Heart failure for nebivolol and carvedilol in selected patients

cards.front: Classify: Antihypertensives in pregnancy
cards.text: {{Methyldopa}} has the longest safety record in pregnancy, {{labetalol}} is the most widely used oral agent, and {{ACE inhibitors}} and {{ARBs}} must be avoided because of fetal damage.

cards.front: Classify: Intravenous agents in hypertensive emergency
cards.text: IV agents used in hypertensive emergency include {{nicardipine}}, {{labetalol}}, {{esmolol}} and {{glyceryl trinitrate}}; {{sodium nitroprusside}} is avoided in stroke and in {{eclampsia}}.

cards.front: How is a hypertensive emergency defined, and name its major indications.
cards.back: BP above about 220 systolic or 120 diastolic with active target-organ damage. Typical settings: stroke or head injury, acute LVF with pulmonary oedema, ACS or MI, aortic dissection, acute renal failure, eclampsia, and pheochromocytoma, cheese reaction or clonidine withdrawal. The organ damage, not the number alone, makes it an emergency needing controlled IV therapy.

cards.front: Sodium nitroprusside: why it suits hypertensive emergencies, and what limits its use.
cards.back: It acts within seconds and wears off within minutes, so BP can be titrated by the infusion rate. It dilates both arterioles and veins, and its NO release does not produce nitrate-type tolerance. Cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity, lactic acidosis, and the need for an infusion pump and arterial monitoring limit its use. It should be avoided in stroke and in eclampsia.

cards.front: Short note: Hypertensive emergency and hypertensive urgency

points: Emergency: BP above 220 systolic or 120 diastolic with active target-organ damage
Urgency: similar BP without acute target-organ damage
Stroke or head injury, hypertensive encephalopathy, acute LVF with pulmonary oedema
ACS, aortic dissection, acute renal failure, eclampsia
Pheochromocytoma, cheese reaction, clonidine withdrawal
Lower mean BP by up to 25% over minutes to 1 to 2 hours, then gradually to about 160/100 mm Hg
Avoid a rapid or excessive fall: risk of ischaemia, infarction and blindness
Nicardipine: widely used; add a beta blocker in ACS to blunt reflex tachycardia
Labetalol: useful in hyperadrenergic states; avoid in heart failure and asthma
Esmolol: aortic dissection; GTN: ACS and acute heart failure
Nitroprusside: mainly aortic dissection; avoid in stroke
Other parenteral options: clevidipine, enalaprilat, fenoldopam, hydralazine and phentolamine
Oral labetalol or amlodipine over hours to days
Oral clonidine and captopril are not favoured

cards.front: Short note: Antihypertensive treatment in pregnancy

points: Continue existing therapy, or switch a harmful drug to a safer one
Target systolic below 150 and diastolic 80 to 100 mm Hg; avoid a rapid fall, which can reduce uteroplacental flow
ACE inhibitors and ARBs: fetal damage and growth retardation
Diuretics: reduce volume and may worsen uteroplacental perfusion
Nonselective beta blockers such as propranolol: low birth weight, neonatal bradycardia
Sodium nitroprusside in eclampsia
Labetalol (oral): most widely used
Methyldopa: longest safety record
Sustained-release nifedipine: stop before labour as it can weaken contractions
Hydralazine: safe but not favoured now
Hydralazine IV is useful in hypertensive emergencies of pre-eclampsia

Low-dose aspirin for women at high risk (diabetes, CKD, chronic hypertension, hypertension in an earlier pregnancy): KDT gives 80 to 100 mg daily from the 12th week until delivery; GG14 cites 81 or 100 mg started early, which reduces preterm pre-eclampsia
Thought to act by inhibiting TXA2 synthesis; evening dosing may give a larger effect

cards.front: Case: hypertensive emergency with acute coronary syndrome. Choose an IV agent and explain how to handle its reflex effect.
cards.back: Nicardipine IV is a popular choice, now replacing nitroprusside; it is a vasoselective DHP with a half-life of about 45 min and an action lasting 3-4 h, and in a trial matched nitroprusside in reaching target BP within an hour. Its vasodilatation causes reflex tachycardia, which is harmful in ACS or MI, so esmolol or labetalol is co-administered.

cards.front: What is the angina index and why does it matter?
cards.back: Heart rate multiplied by systolic BP. It tracks myocardial oxygen consumption, and each patient has a threshold at which angina starts.

cards.front: What is the subendocardial crunch in an attack of angina?
cards.back: The ischaemic ventricle's end-diastolic pressure rises (about 5 to 25 mm Hg), so subendocardial blood flow, which occurs only in diastole, falls. Drugs that lower preload relieve it.

cards.front: Thallium-201 and Tc-99m pyrophosphate in myocardial ischaemia: where does each localise?
cards.back: Thallium-201 localises to well-perfused myocardium, so ischaemia shows as a defect. Tc-99m pyrophosphate localises to necrosed myocardium.

cards.front: Computerised exercise stress test for an antianginal: what is the outcome measure?
cards.back: Exercise tolerance before pain and ECG change appear. A drug that delays both shows antianginal activity when the test is repeated after dosing.

cards.front: What does a Langendorff preparation measure in cardiac screening?
cards.back: An isolated perfused heart, perfused retrograde. It records inotropic and chronotropic effects and coronary resistance from the rate of drip collection.

cards.front: Tail-cuff method in rodents: what does it measure and what limits it?
cards.back: Non-invasive systolic BP in conscious or unconscious rats and mice. Restraint stress can produce misleading readings.

cards.front: DOCA-salt model: how is hypertension produced in rats?
cards.back: DOCA 20 mg/kg s.c. with saline as drinking water for about four weeks. Sodium and water retention raise volume and sympathetic and RAAS activity.

cards.front: Which agent, given at high dose, produces experimental acute MI in animals?
cards.back: Isoprenaline (isoproterenol). Its strong beta-1 action causes myocyte necrosis.

cards.front: Why must a controlled trial be used to judge an antianginal drug?
cards.back: Placebo responses are 30 to 80% in chronic stable angina, so an apparent benefit can be a placebo effect.

cards.front: Crossover trial design: which chronic conditions suit it?
cards.back: Chronic stable disease such as hypertension or stable angina, where the baseline is reached at the start of each treatment arm.

cards.front: Why is acetazolamide not used as a diuretic today?
cards.back: Its diuresis is self-limiting. Bicarbonate loss causes acidosis and hypokalaemia, so it is used for glaucoma, urinary alkalinisation, adjunct epilepsy and altitude sickness.

cards.front: Spironolactone: why is it a weak diuretic yet useful in combination?
cards.back: It antagonises aldosterone in the late distal tubule, where most Na+ is already reabsorbed. It conserves K+ and offsets the K+ loss caused by thiazide and loop diuretics.

cards.front: Digoxin: which enzyme does it inhibit, and what is its main clinical role?
cards.back: Na+/K+-ATPase. Positive inotropy in heart failure and ventricular rate control in atrial fibrillation.

cards.front: Digoxin therapeutic window: what does the DIG trial show?
cards.back: Benefit at about 0.5 to 0.8 ng/mL. Concentrations of 1.2 ng/mL and above tend to link to higher mortality.

cards.front: Why is oral minoxidil no longer used?
cards.back: Vasodilatation is marked and the reflex effects are strong. Risk of ischaemia and heart failure is high. Topical 2% is used for alopecia.

cards.front: What did the IONA trial show for nicorandil?
cards.back: Fewer acute coronary events in high-risk patients with stable angina.

cards.front: Thiazide diuretics: what is the effect on glucose tolerance?
cards.back: They can worsen glucose tolerance and precipitate diabetes. Low-dose thiazides still benefit more than this risk, so they are not contraindicated in diabetics.

cards.front: Short note: Evaluation of antianginal drugs (experimental methods)

points: Animal coronary data often do not carry over to humans
Isolated hearts show responses that differ from the intact body
Langendorff retrograde perfusion
Records inotropy, chronotropy and coronary resistance (drop count)
High-dose isoprenaline gives acute MI by myocyte necrosis
Infarct graded on histology

cards.front: Short note: Evaluation of antianginal drugs (clinical methods)

points: Exercise tolerance before pain and ECG change
Repeat after the drug; a delay shows activity
Thallium-201 perfusion; Tc-99m pyrophosphate for necrosis
Coronary angiography, with pharmacological or exercise stress
Placebo response 30 to 80% in stable angina, so controls are needed
Crossover suits chronic stable disease

cards.front: Short note: Non-haemodynamic antianginal drugs

points: Act without changing heart rate or BP at rest or on exercise
Reduce angina and improve exercise capacity
Inhibits long-chain 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (LC3-KAT)
Shifts myocardial fuel from fatty acid to glucose, so less O2 is needed per ATP
Labelled a pFOX inhibitor; add-on therapy
Inhibits late Na+ current, which lowers Ca2+ overload
No effect on HR or BP; prolongs exercise duration
Prolongs QT; avoid CYP3A4 inhibitors

cards.front: Essay: Weak diuretics

points: Diuretics with low natriuretic power
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and spironolactone are the examples
Block CA II and IV in proximal tubule, so HCO3- and Na+ reabsorption fall
Alkaline, K+-rich urine; maximal natriuresis is small
Diuresis is self-limiting; acidosis and hypokalaemia follow
Uses: glaucoma, urine alkalinisation, adjunct in absence seizures, altitude sickness
Avoid in liver disease (hepatic coma risk); acidosis is more likely in COPD
Competitive aldosterone antagonist acting from the interstitial side of the late distal tubule
Mild saluretic; conserves K+ and offsets diuretic-induced K+ loss
Onset 3 to 4 days; canrenone is the main active metabolite
Uses: refractory oedema (cirrhosis, nephrotic), resistant hypertension, heart failure
Weak in their own right, useful as adjuncts to thiazide or loop diuretics

cards.front: Short note: Digoxin

points: Inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase; raised intracellular Ca2+ gives positive inotropy
Vagotonic: slows AV conduction and so controls ventricular rate
Symptomatic heart failure, now not first choice
Rate control in atrial fibrillation
Loading dose about 0.6 to 1 mg over 24 h
Maintenance to serum level 0.5 to 2 ng/mL; monitor levels
Narrow therapeutic index; arrhythmias most serious
Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and renal impairment raise risk
DIG trial: fewer HF hospitalisations with no rise in mortality
Beneficial range 0.5 to 0.8 ng/mL; 1.2 ng/mL and above linked to higher mortality

cards.front: Short note: Evaluation of antihypertensive agents

points: Tail-cuff systolic BP in rats; telemetry for conscious animals
DOCA-salt model: volume and RAAS-driven hypertension over about 4 weeks
Judge by BP change, ECG, and histology of the heart
Efficacy judged on morbidity and mortality endpoints in large randomised trials
Effective BP lowering cuts stroke by 30 to 50%, heart failure by 40 to 50%, CAD by about 15%
Placebo control and crossover where the disease is chronic and stable
JNC 8 treatment threshold of 150 mm Hg systolic at age 60 and above

cards.front: Essay: Pharmacology of vasodilator drugs used in therapeutics

points: Nitrates and nitroprusside: NO donors, mainly venodilator or balanced
Hydralazine: direct arteriolar dilator
Minoxidil, diazoxide, nicorandil: K-ATP channel openers
Nicardipine IV: vasoselective dihydropyridine
Arteriolar dilators cause reflex tachycardia, renin release and fluid retention
Nitrates reduce preload first; coronary steal possible with nitroprusside
Angina: nitrates, nicorandil
Hypertension: hydralazine as second line; pregnancy (pre-eclampsia)
Emergencies: nicardipine first, nitroprusside second line
Heart failure: hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate; nitroprusside in refractory cases
Topical minoxidil for alopecia
Hydralazine: lupus-like syndrome above about 100 mg/day, more in women and slow acetylators
Nitroprusside: cyanide, then thiocyanate accumulation; light-protected infusion
Minoxidil: fluid retention, hirsutism, ischaemia; avoid oral use

cards.front: Essay: Pathophysiology of myocardial ischaemia and the drugs that modulate it

points: Angina is a supply and demand mismatch in part of the myocardium
Fixed atherosclerotic stenosis, or coronary vasospasm, limits supply
Demand rises with heart rate, systolic BP, contractility and size
Angina index is heart rate times systolic BP
Metabolites accumulate and elicit pain
End-diastolic pressure rises; subendocardial crunch and transient LV failure follow
Nitrates: preload and afterload fall, so wall tension and O2 use fall; subendocardial flow improves
Beta blockers: lower HR, contractility and BP, so demand falls; no coronary dilatation
Calcium channel blockers: dihydropyridines dilate and reduce afterload; verapamil and diltiazem slow HR
Nicorandil: K-ATP opener and NO donor; trimetazidine and ranolazine act on metabolism and late Na+ current; ivabradine lowers HR only
Antianginals relieve ischaemia but do not change CAD; aspirin, ACE inhibitors and statins modify it

cards.front: Essay: Impact of comorbidity on the choice of antihypertensive drugs

points: Use compelling indications first, otherwise age and race
Non-black young patients respond better to ACE inhibitors or ARBs; older and black patients respond better to CCBs
Heart failure: diuretic, ACE inhibitor or ARB, beta blocker
Post-MI: ACE inhibitor or ARB, beta blocker
High CAD risk: ACE inhibitor, CCB, diuretic
Diabetes: ACE inhibitor or ARB; CCB; avoid beta blocker with diuretic (diabetes risk)
CKD: ACE inhibitor or ARB
Resistant hypertension with diabetes or CKD: add aldosterone antagonist if K+ below 4.5 mmol/L
Recurrent stroke: diuretic, ACE inhibitor or ARB, CCB
Pregnancy: avoid ACE inhibitors and ARBs; methyldopa and hydralazine used; diuretics avoided in toxaemia
Avoid verapamil or diltiazem with a beta blocker (bradycardia, AV block)
Amlodipine with lisinopril or enalapril (ACE inhibitor combinations)
Losartan with amlodipine, a fixed ARB and CCB combination
Amlodipine with atenolol, a CCB and beta blocker combination; avoid verapamil or diltiazem with beta blockers
Enalapril or losartan with hydrochlorothiazide when a diuretic is needed for heart failure or oedema

cards.front: Working myocardium versus automatic fibres: what separates them?
cards.back: Working (non-automatic) fibres hold a stable resting potential of about -90 mV and cannot fire on their own. Automatic fibres in the SA and AV nodes and His-Purkinje system show slow phase-4 depolarisation and generate their own impulses.

cards.front: Which ion carries phase 0 in fast-channel versus slow-channel action potentials?
cards.back: Fast-channel fibres (atria, ventricles, Purkinje) depolarise through Na+ entry. Slow-channel fibres (SA and AV nodes) depolarise through Ca2+ entry, which is slower and has a less negative threshold.

cards.front: Why is conduction slow in SA and AV nodal tissue?
cards.back: Slow-channel action potentials have a slow 0 phase, low amplitude and small overshoot, so the wave moves decrementally. Conduction velocity is about 0.01 to 0.1 m/s in slow-channel tissue against 0.5 to 5 m/s in fast-channel tissue.

cards.front: How do effective refractory period and action potential duration compare in fast-channel and slow-channel fibres?
cards.back: Fast-channel fibres recover Na+ channels voltage-dependently, so ERP is shorter than APD (ERP/APD below 1). Slow-channel fibres recover Ca2+ channels with time, so ERP is longer than APD (ERP/APD above 1).

cards.front: Which tissue is the normal pacemaker, and what is its key feature?
cards.back: The SA node. It has the steepest phase-4 slope and so reaches threshold first. Other automatic tissue fires more slowly and acts as latent pacemaker if the SA node fails.

cards.front: How does hyperpolarisation change excitability, and what happens below about -55 mV?
cards.back: Hyperpolarisation widens the gap to threshold, so the fibre is less excitable. Below about -55 mV in fast-channel fibres, all Na+ channels are inactivated and the fibre cannot respond.

cards.front: Vagal (ACh) versus sympathetic (adrenaline) effects on the heart: automaticity, refractoriness, conduction and contractility.
cards.back: Vagal stimulation slows SA automaticity, shortens atrial refractoriness, prolongs refractoriness in conducting tissue and depresses conduction. Sympathetic stimulation increases automaticity and contractility, shortens refractoriness and enhances conduction.

cards.front: Short note: Normal cardiac electrophysiology

points: Working fibres: stable resting potential, no self-excitation
Automatic fibres (SA, AV, His-Purkinje): phase-4 slow depolarisation
Fast-channel: Na+ current, fast 0 phase, threshold near -60 to -70 mV
Slow-channel: Ca2+ current, slow 0 phase, threshold near -45 to -55 mV
Conduction depends on membrane responsiveness at the resting potential
ERP is the key refractory measure; ERP/APD is below 1 in fast-channel and above 1 in slow-channel tissue
Vagal: slows SA firing, prolongs AV refractoriness
Sympathetic: raises automaticity, conduction and contractility
Most antiarrhythmics increase ERP/APD
Drugs that reduce the 0-phase slope shift the responsiveness curve to the right and slow conduction

cards.front: Essay: Normal electrophysiological properties of the myocardium and their link to antiarrhythmic drug action

points: Working and automatic myocardial fibres
Four properties: impulse generation, conduction, excitability, refractoriness
Phase 0 to 4 in working fibres
Phase-4 slope and threshold set the firing rate; SA node is the pacemaker
Fast-channel (Na+) versus slow-channel (Ca2+) tissue
Membrane responsiveness depends on resting potential; -55 mV inactivates all Na+ channels
ERP is the key measure; ERP/APD below 1 in fast tissue and above 1 in slow tissue
Most antiarrhythmics raise ERP/APD
Vagal action slows SA firing and depresses AV conduction
Sympathetic action increases automaticity and conduction
Class I reduces the 0-phase slope and slows conduction in fast tissue
Class IV (verapamil, diltiazem) blocks slow-channel tissue; class III prolongs ERP
